definition: Baseline check for any output before it is used: (1) Factually correct? Do facts, figures, dates and names hold? (2) Complete? Is a relevant aspect missing? (3) Appropriate? Does the tone fit, and does the wording carry discriminatory claims? Review depth and additional controls follow purpose and impact.
A natural or legal person that develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name (EU AI Act Art. 3(3)).
Computes weighted relationships between token representations. It helps transformer models connect context; it establishes neither relevance nor understanding.
A contract under GDPR Art. 28 when a controller engages a processor to process personal data. Whether a DPA is required, and whether it is enough, follows from the roles and the processing.

Rights of natural persons under the GDPR: access (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), objection (Art. 21). They apply when AI systems process personal data too.
A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority; personal non-professional activity is excluded (EU AI Act Art. 3(4)).

A systematic deviation that can come from data collection, labels, objectives, modeling, evaluation or deployment context. It can affect groups differently. Discrimination does not follow automatically.
The EU AI Act records kept together: AI inventory, risk classifications, training records, usage policies, incident-response protocols. It supports documentation. It replaces no legal review.
The field of AI that processes and analyzes images and video. Face recognition, quality control, autonomous driving.

An assessment under GDPR Art. 35 when planned processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. AI can be a risk factor. It does not trigger a DPIA automatically.
An example model that sorts company data into four protection levels. The organization sets labels, criteria and permitted workflows; the level alone approves no product.
A branch of machine learning built on artificial neural networks with many layers. It makes pattern recognition possible in complex data such as images, speech and text.

AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles real people, objects, places or events and can falsely appear authentic. The legal definition follows the applicable framework.
Further training of a pretrained model on selected data or preferences, to adjust its behavior for particular tasks or domains. Separate evaluations have to show whether it worked.
AI systems that produce new content: text, images, audio, video, code. ChatGPT, DALL-E, Midjourney, Claude.
Output from a generative model that looks plausible and is unsupported, inconsistent or factually wrong. Language-model generation carries no automatic fact check.

An AI system classified as high-risk under Art. 6 in conjunction with Annex I or III. Provider duties and deployer duties differ. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems integrated into products.

A design in which people hold defined monitoring, intervention or decision authority. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems; a human final decision is not shaped identically in every use case.
The process in which a trained model takes an input and produces an output. Every ChatGPT answer is an inference.

Skills, knowledge and understanding that allow informed AI use and awareness of opportunities, risks and possible harm (EU AI Act Art. 3(56)). Article 4 requires context-specific measures supporting the development of this literacy.
A machine-based system that turns inputs into outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions, and can work at varying levels of autonomy (EU AI Act Art. 3(1)).

The procedure that checks whether a high-risk AI system meets the requirements applying to it. Procedure and involvement of a notified body follow the system and the legal basis; CE marking follows only where the framework provides for it.
An umbrella term for machine-based systems that derive outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions from inputs. The exact definition follows the technical or legal context.

A large model for token sequences, trained on extensive data, that models probabilities over outputs. Depending on the model it handles modalities beyond text. Product name and model version are two different things.

The field of AI in which model parameters are adjusted from data and optimization objectives. Supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning are common categories, not a closed list.
The trained result of a machine-learning process. It holds the learned parameters, the weights, and applies to new inputs.
The field of AI that processes natural language: translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, text generation.
A computational model modeled on biological neurons. Layers of connected nodes. The basis of deep learning.
A model fits the peculiarities or noise of the training data too closely and generalizes worse to new data. Memorization can be a symptom, and is not the only form.
Values a model adjusts during training, such as weights and bias terms. Parameter count alone compares neither quality nor cost nor suitability.
The input to a generative system: instruction, question, data, context. A clear prompt can shape the output. Correctness and quality it does not settle.

A versioned collection of prompt templates for recurring tasks, with purpose, permitted inputs, example outputs, review steps and evaluation results. Benefit and limits get measured in the actual process.

An attack or failure mode in which instructions inside user input or processed content push a model outside its intended behavior. OWASP lists Prompt Injection as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications.

A pattern in which a generative model receives retrieved content as context. It can improve traceability and factual accuracy. It depends on retrieval, source quality and correct use, and it prevents no hallucinations.
A course template with the fields Role, Context, Task, Format and Constraints. It makes requirements visible. Not every task needs every field, and the template guarantees no correct output.
A type of machine learning in which an agent learns by trial and error. Reward for wanted behavior, penalty for unwanted. Robotics, game strategies.
Use of AI services or features outside the approved inventory and the intended controls. Consumer offers, extensions, embedded features, local models.
A type of machine learning that works from labeled training data. The model learns the mapping from input to output through examples. Spam filters, credit scoring, image recognition.
The smallest unit an LLM processes. A word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark. Models generate text token by token.
The data used to adjust model parameters. Selection, quality, representativeness and documentation shape behavior; model, objective, evaluation and deployment context shape it too.

A neural-network architecture presented in 2017 that uses attention and positional information. It carries many current language models and allows highly parallel training. Modern models are not all built identically.
A type of machine learning without labeled data. The model finds patterns and structures on its own. Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, clustering.
